title: The Terminal and the Filesystem Hierarchy
objectives: Explain what the shell is and how it relates to the kernel
Navigate the filesystem using absolute and relative paths, ., .. and ~
Locate the standard roles of /etc, /var, /home, /opt, /tmp and /proc in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard
Inspect files and directories with ls, cat, head, tail, wc and glob patterns
motivation: First day on the desk: 'fill logs are in /var/log/quant, config in /etc/quant, the engine runs from /opt/quant, go find out why fills stopped.' There is no GUI on a production server and no search engine for your own filesystem. Everything on Linux hangs off one root directory, and the terminal is the only reliable way to walk it, so we learn the tree and the handful of commands that move through it.

blocks.text: The shell: a conversation with the kernel

blocks.md: A **terminal** is a window into a **shell**, a program (usually bash) that reads a line, parses it into a command plus arguments, asks the kernel to run it, and prints the result, then repeats. That read-evaluate-print loop is why the shell feels like a conversation. The shell is also a full language (loops, variables, exit codes, the next lessons), and because servers are administered over SSH with no desktop, terminal fluency is not optional for a quant developer.

blocks.caption: whoami: which user am I; pwd: print working directory; SHELL: which shell is running.

blocks.md: Linux has no drive letters. There is exactly one hierarchy beginning at **/** (the root), and other disks or network shares are **mounted** onto directories within it, blending invisibly into the tree. Paths come in two flavours: **absolute** paths start at / and work from anywhere; **relative** paths start where you are, using **.** for here, **..** for the parent, and **~** for your home directory.

rows: Executable programs the system provides (ls, grep, python3)
System and service configuration, as plain text files
Optional third-party software, often one directory per product
Kernel and process information exposed as virtual files
Scratch space; typically wiped on reboot, never store state here
Variable data: logs under /var/log, queues, spools

blocks.md: Learn the roles, not an exhaustive map. When the lead says 'config lives in /etc/quant', you know exactly what kind of thing to expect: text files you can read and diff. When a log floods the disk, you look in /var/log first. These conventions (the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard) are why any Linux box feels familiar within minutes.

blocks.code:
$ cd /opt/quant && ls
engine  feed  tools
$ cd feed
$ pwd
/opt/quant/feed
$ ls -F
config.yaml  fills.csv  run.sh*
$ head -n 3 fills.csv
time,symbol,side,qty,price
09:30:01.123,AAPL,BUY,100,187.42
09:30:01.456,MSFT,SELL,50,415.10
blocks.caption: A trading repo as the shell sees it; ls -F marks executables with a star.

blocks.md: A small inspection toolkit covers most questions: **ls -l** for details, **cat** for whole small files, **head -n 3** and **tail -n 5** for first and last lines (tail -f follows a growing log, the monitoring lesson uses it constantly), **wc -l** to count lines, and **file** to ask what kind of thing a path actually is. **Globs** let the shell expand patterns before a command runs: *.csv becomes every CSV in the current directory.

blocks.code:
$ wc -l fills.csv
4 fills.csv
$ tail -n 1 fills.csv
09:30:02.001,AAPL,BUY,200,187.44
$ ls *.csv
fills.csv  positions.csv
blocks.caption: wc counts lines (header plus three fills); globs expand before ls even runs.

steps.note: Print working directory, where am I?
A file: type, permissions, owner, group, size, mtime, name.

out: hier, description of the filesystem hierarchy

blocks.title: Paths you will live in
blocks.md: Production conventions repeat across desks: services under /opt/name, config under /etc/name, logs under /var/log/name, scratch in /tmp (with the reboot caveat). Knowing the convention, you can navigate an unfamiliar trading server on day one, and you will know that a 100 GB log hiding in /var/log is what pages someone at 3am.

One directory breaks the rules beautifully: **/proc** is not files on a disk but a window the kernel renders on the fly. /proc/self is the current process; /proc/self/status holds its memory and signal state; /proc/cpuinfo describes the CPUs. Reading a file there triggers the kernel to generate fresh content, the first hint that on Linux 'everything is a file' is an interface design, a theme the OS lessons develop.

guidedExercise.prompt: You are in /opt/quant/feed. (1) Give one relative and one absolute path that reach /opt/quant/tools. (2) Write a single command showing the last 5 lines of /var/log/quant/fills.log. (3) What does cd .. do from /opt/quant/feed?
hints: Relative paths climb with ..; absolute paths start at /.
tail prints the end of a file; -n 5 sets the count.
guidedExercise.solution: (1) Relative: ../tools; absolute: /opt/quant/tools. (2) tail -n 5 /var/log/quant/fills.log. (3) It moves to the parent directory /opt/quant, since .. always means 'one level up'.

independentExercise.prompt: Your ~/data directory holds trades_2026-01.csv through trades_2026-12.csv plus notes.txt. (1) Write a glob that matches only the January-to-March files. (2) Write one command that counts the lines of those three files at once and reports a total. (3) Why is putting your results in /tmp a bad idea?
hints: wc accepts multiple files and prints a total line.
independentExercise.solution: (1) ls ~/data/trades_2026-0[1-3].csv. (2) wc -l ~/data/trades_2026-0[1-3].csv, prints each file's count plus a total. (3) /tmp is world-writable scratch that many systems clear on reboot and that other users can read; results (and anything sensitive) belong under your home or the project directory with proper permissions.

commonMistakes: Unquoted paths with spaces: cd My Reports fails; quote it: cd 'My Reports'.
Storing state in /tmp and losing it at reboot, or letting other users read it.
Confusing ~ (your home directory) with / (the root of the whole system).
Typing absolute paths everywhere when relative paths (../tools) make scripts portable between checkouts.
realWorldApplication: Server administration, Docker images, CI runners and HPC clusters all assume FHS fluency; 'check /var/log' is the universal first move of incident response on Linux.
quantFinanceApplication: Trading infrastructure follows the same conventions, engines in /opt, config in /etc, logs in /var/log, and feed outages are diagnosed by walking exactly these paths under time pressure.
summary: The shell is a read-evaluate-print loop in front of the kernel; the terminal is the universal interface to Linux servers.
Everything hangs under one root /; other devices are mounted into the tree; absolute paths start at /, relative paths use . and ..
The FHS gives predictable roles: /etc config, /var/log logs, /opt add-on software, /tmp scratch, /proc a live kernel window.
head, tail, cat, wc and globs answer most inspection questions in one line each.

quiz.prompt: Which directory holds system configuration files?
quiz.explanation: /etc is the FHS home for configuration; /bin holds executables, /home user data, /tmp scratch.
.. climbs to /opt/quant, then tools descends into /opt/quant/tools.
printf emits two newline characters, so the stream has two lines and wc -l counts 2.

quiz.prompt: Why do servers run headless with shell access rather than desktops?
quiz.modelAnswer: GUIs consume memory and CPU, cannot be used comfortably over remote links, and cannot be automated; the shell works over SSH, scripts well, and needs no display.
quiz.explanation: Headless servers save resources and enable automation, both essential at scale.

quiz.prompt: Which of these are absolute paths?
quiz.explanation: Absolute paths begin with /, describing location from the root regardless of the current directory. ~/notes.txt is home-relative and ../data is current-directory-relative.

quiz.prompt: What does this command sequence print?
quiz.explanation: cd log moves into /var/log, then cd .. returns to the parent /var, which pwd prints.

flashcards.back: A program (e.g. bash) that reads a command line, parses it, asks the kernel to execute it and prints results, also a full scripting language.
Absolute starts at / and works from anywhere; relative starts at the current directory using . and ..; ~ means your home.
A virtual filesystem the kernel generates on demand, exposing process and hardware state as readable files.
Moves to /opt/quant/tools, .. climbs one level, then descends into the sibling.
